title: Recombinant DNA Technology and Molecular Testing — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Recombinant DNA Technology lecture and Nucleic Acid Metabolism lectures

questions.stem: What is a restriction endonuclease primarily used for in recombinant DNA construction?

options.label: A
options.text: Translating RNA into amino acid chains

options.label: D
options.text: Joining amino acids by peptide bonds

questions.why: A restriction endonuclease recognises a particular motif in DNA and cleaves the DNA at or near that site. Different recognition motifs account for differences in cutting patterns.

notes.A: Translation is performed by ribosomes and produces polypeptides rather than cleaved DNA fragments.
notes.C: A poly-A tail is added to RNA by a different enzyme during transcript processing.
notes.D: Peptide-bond formation links amino acids at ribosomes, while restriction cleavage acts on DNA.
notes.E: ATP production from ADP is an energy metabolism process rather than a consequence of sequence-specific DNA cleavage.

questions.stem: Why can bacteria protect their own DNA from certain endogenous restriction enzymes?

options.label: C
options.text: Their DNA lacks all recognition sequences

questions.why: In a typical restriction–modification system, the matching methyltransferase marks host recognition sites. The endogenous restriction enzyme generally distinguishes those modified sites from susceptible unmodified ones.

notes.A: A bacterial chromosome has a sugar–phosphate backbone like other DNA.
notes.B: Bacterial DNA has the usual DNA bases, including thymine rather than uracil as its standard partner for adenine.
notes.C: Recognition sites can occur in the host chromosome. Modification can protect them even when they are present.
notes.E: Typical bacterial plasmids are DNA, and the protection described is a modification of DNA.

questions.stem: Which enzyme covalently joins a gene insert to the DNA backbone of a cut plasmid?
questions.why: DNA ligase makes phosphodiester bonds between adjacent DNA ends. This seals the insert and the plasmid backbone into a covalently continuous DNA molecule.

notes.B: DNA helicase separates paired strands. It does not make the bonds joining the insert to the backbone.
notes.C: Primase makes a short RNA primer rather than covalently closing a nick in DNA.
notes.D: Ribonuclease H removes RNA from RNA–DNA hybrids and does not ligate two DNA ends.
notes.E: Topoisomerase I transiently cleaves and reseals a strand to alter topology rather than joining inserts to vectors.

questions.stem: Which plasmid feature permits autonomous replication after introduction into bacteria?
questions.why: A plasmid origin of replication is a site where compatible replication machinery can initiate copying of the plasmid. This allows maintenance as a DNA molecule separate from the chromosome.

notes.A: A poly-A tail is an RNA feature and does not provide a site for plasmid replication.
notes.B: A stop codon is a translation signal that terminates protein synthesis rather than initiating DNA copying.
notes.D: Bacteria lack a host-cell nucleus. Autonomous plasmid replication depends on an origin recognised within the cell.
notes.E: RNA splicing and ribosome function do not provide a DNA replication initiation site.

questions.stem: What is a selectable marker in an expression plasmid commonly used to do?

options.label: C
options.text: Change the genetic code of host cells

questions.why: A selectable marker gives cells carrying the vector a distinguishable trait. This allows them to be identified by their response to an appropriate selection condition.

notes.A: The marker is used to distinguish cells carrying the vector rather than modify intron length.
notes.B: A restriction endonuclease cleaves DNA at recognition sites, whereas a marker is a selectable genetic trait.
notes.C: A selectable marker does not change the host's genetic code. It gives cells a specific identifiable property.
notes.D: Selected cells must remain capable of growth, which generally requires continued expression of chromosomal genes.

questions.stem: Which method directly introduces plasmid DNA into bacterial cells by short electrical pulses?
questions.why: In electroporation, an electrical pulse transiently increases membrane permeability. This can allow DNA to enter cells while leaving viable cells able to reseal their membranes.

notes.A: Southern blotting detects particular DNA sequences after separation and transfer, rather than introducing DNA into living cells.
notes.C: Northern blotting measures RNA transcripts using hybridisation and is not a DNA delivery method.
notes.D: Peptide sequencing determines the order of amino acid residues rather than delivering a plasmid.
notes.E: Density-gradient centrifugation separates material by physical properties rather than making membranes permeable to DNA.

questions.stem: Which vector combines features of plasmids and bacteriophage lambda to accommodate relatively large inserts?
questions.why: A cosmid is a plasmid-derived vector containing bacteriophage lambda cos sites. These features distinguish it from a simple plasmid and permit cloning of relatively large DNA inserts.

notes.A: A simple plasmid may replicate in bacteria but does not necessarily contain the lambda cos sites that define a cosmid.
notes.B: A PCR primer is a short oligonucleotide used for synthesis rather than a cloning vector.
notes.C: Mature mRNA is a transcript and lacks the plasmid and phage features needed to define a cosmid.
notes.E: A restriction enzyme cuts DNA. The genetic material being maintained is carried by a vector.

questions.stem: Which vector is designed to carry very large cloned DNA fragments in a bacterial host?
questions.why: A bacterial artificial chromosome is built to maintain long genomic DNA segments in bacteria. Its insert capacity is much greater than that of conventional small cloning plasmids.

notes.B: Conventional plasmids are useful for relatively small inserts and generally lack the capacity of bacterial artificial chromosomes.
notes.C: A short tRNA sequence is an insert, not a vehicle that maintains large genomic fragments.
notes.D: A primer supplies an end for DNA synthesis and does not act as a large-insert cloning vector.
notes.E: A bacteriophage coat protein contributes to a viral shell rather than independently maintaining a DNA insert in cells.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a shuttle vector from a vector limited to one host species?

options.label: E
options.text: A requirement for only RNA inserts

questions.why: A shuttle vector contains features enabling it to replicate or be maintained in two different host types. It can therefore carry the same cloned material between them.

notes.A: Replication or maintenance features recognised in each host are needed, rather than absence of all origins.
notes.B: Selectable markers can be useful in either host. Their absence is not a defining property of shuttle vectors.
notes.D: Translation produces protein, but a shuttle vector is defined by the ability to propagate in different hosts.
notes.E: Shuttle vectors are DNA constructs and are not defined by a requirement to carry only RNA inserts.

questions.stem: Why is complementary DNA often preferred for expressing human insulin in bacteria?

options.label: C
options.text: It is made only from proteins

questions.why: A DNA copy of processed insulin mRNA already contains the coding exons joined together. This avoids depending on bacteria to remove the intervening sequences of the human gene.

notes.A: Coding exons are retained in cDNA made from processed insulin mRNA.
notes.B: The cDNA sequence can be transcribed when it is expressed from a compatible promoter.
notes.C: A cDNA molecule is copied from RNA by reverse transcription and cannot be made from protein sequence directly.
notes.D: An insert can be carried by a plasmid. Destruction of the plasmid is not the reason for choosing cDNA.

questions.stem: Which enzyme converts a mature messenger RNA template into complementary DNA?
questions.why: Reverse transcriptase synthesises DNA from an RNA template. The product is complementary DNA corresponding to the sequence of the copied messenger RNA.

notes.A: DNA ligase joins adjacent DNA ends but does not copy information from an RNA template.
notes.C: RNA polymerase II usually transcribes DNA into RNA, the opposite template and product types from those asked for.
notes.D: A restriction endonuclease recognises and cuts motifs in DNA, without synthesising a complementary strand.
notes.E: Primase synthesises a short RNA primer from a DNA template rather than making a DNA copy of RNA.

questions.stem: What is a major difference between a genomic DNA library and a cDNA library?

options.label: A
options.text: Genomic libraries contain only translated exons

options.label: B
options.text: cDNA libraries contain all chromosomal promoters

options.label: C
options.text: cDNA libraries contain all telomeric repeats

options.label: D
options.text: Genomic libraries preserve introns and flanks

options.label: E
options.text: Both libraries are limited to plasmid RNA only

questions.why: A genomic library represents chromosomal DNA, so it can retain introns and sequences flanking genes. A library copied from mature mRNA instead represents processed expressed transcripts.

notes.A: Genomic DNA includes introns and intergenic regions in addition to coding exons.
notes.B: Promoters are generally upstream of the transcribed sequence and are not systematically represented in mature-mRNA cDNA.
notes.C: Chromosomal telomeric repeats are not generally represented by libraries made from mature mRNA.
notes.E: Both libraries contain DNA inserts. A cDNA library is derived from RNA rather than storing only plasmid RNA.

questions.stem: Which property makes a cDNA library dependent on the tissue and condition sampled?

options.label: B
options.text: It contains all loci at equal abundance

options.label: C
options.text: It requires loss of the ribosomal code

questions.why: A cDNA library made from messenger RNA reflects which transcripts are present and their relative levels in the sample. Tissue and physiological state both influence that population.

notes.B: Genes expressed at different levels are represented differently, and unexpressed loci can be missing.
notes.C: The genetic code remains intact. The variable is which transcripts were present when the sample was taken.
notes.D: cDNA can represent many nuclear-encoded transcripts and is not limited to mitochondrial sequences.
notes.E: Transcript sequences retain gene-specific information, which is why they reveal differences between tissue samples.

questions.stem: Which component defines the two ends of a DNA region amplified in conventional PCR?
questions.why: The forward and reverse primers pair with complementary sites on opposite DNA strands. Their positions define the two boundaries of the region copied during PCR.

notes.A: Antibodies bind antigens and do not serve as primer termini for DNA polymerase.
notes.B: Restriction-enzyme inhibitors do not base-pair with the template to determine the start positions of synthesis.
notes.D: Ribosomal subunits organise translation rather than selecting the ends of a DNA segment for amplification.
notes.E: Collagen chains are proteins and cannot provide sequence-specific DNA primer binding.

questions.stem: Which enzyme property is essential for standard repeated high-temperature PCR cycling?
questions.why: A thermostable DNA polymerase retains sufficient activity after repeated heating used to separate the strands. It can therefore extend primers over successive cycles.

notes.A: A spliceosome processes precursor RNA and does not catalyse DNA synthesis during PCR.
notes.B: Peptide ligation joins amino acid chains, whereas PCR requires synthesis of DNA.
notes.C: Antibody binding does not provide the strand-copying activity required for PCR.
notes.D: Photoreceptor kinase modifies signalling proteins rather than copying a DNA template.

questions.stem: What is the principal purpose of the high-temperature first step in each PCR cycle?

options.label: B
options.text: Separate the two DNA template strands

questions.why: Heating disrupts noncovalent interactions holding the two DNA strands together. The separated strands are then available as templates for subsequent primer binding and copying.

notes.A: Primer annealing occurs after strand separation when conditions favour complementary base pairing.
notes.C: Okazaki fragment joining is part of cellular DNA replication and is not the purpose of the heat step.
notes.D: Poly-A tails occur on RNA and are not extended by denaturing a DNA template.
notes.E: The heat step is used to separate paired strands without intentionally destroying the primers.

questions.stem: What occurs during the annealing phase of a conventional PCR cycle?

options.label: A
options.text: DNA polymerase adds all amino acids

options.label: C
options.text: Taq polymerase removes all target DNA

questions.why: During annealing, each primer can base-pair with a complementary sequence on a separated DNA strand. This provides a defined starting point for subsequent chain extension.

notes.A: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides, not amino acids. The annealing step provides a primer–template duplex.
notes.B: Restriction endonucleases cleave DNA motifs and are distinct from enzymes that methylate DNA.
notes.C: The thermostable polymerase is used subsequently to extend the bound primer rather than remove the template.
notes.E: Ligase repairs certain backbone nicks but does not mediate complementary binding of primers to template.

questions.stem: Why is the extension phase of standard Taq PCR often performed near 72 degrees Celsius?

options.label: A
options.text: It supports DNA extension by Taq polymerase

options.label: B
options.text: It completely denatures the PCR template

options.label: C
options.text: It limits primer binding to single-stranded DNA

options.label: E
options.text: It allows ribosomes to synthesize Taq protein

questions.why: Around the stated temperature, Taq polymerase can efficiently add nucleotides to annealed primers. This supports chain elongation during the extension phase.

notes.B: Complete strand separation is the purpose of a distinct denaturation phase, not the extension phase.
notes.C: Primers bind complementary sequences during annealing. The extension phase supports polymerase catalysis after binding.
notes.D: Plasmid-based resistance is a selectable cell trait, unrelated to extension by Taq polymerase.
notes.E: Taq is already present as an active enzyme. Ribosomes and new protein synthesis are not required for extension.

questions.stem: Under ideal conditions, what is the approximate amplification factor after ten PCR cycles from one double-stranded target?
questions.why: With perfect efficiency, the amount of double-stranded target doubles each cycle. Ten successive doublings give 2 to the tenth power, or 1,024 times the starting amount.

notes.A: Ten squared gives 100, which is not the result of ten doublings.
notes.B: Multiplying two by ten gives a linear estimate. Each cycle doubles the entire amount present from the preceding cycle.
notes.D: Ten to the tenth power assumes a tenfold increase per cycle rather than one doubling.
notes.E: One tenth is a reduction in amount rather than an amplification factor.

questions.stem: Why is conventional PCR poorly suited to amplifying DNA with completely unknown flanking sequences?

options.label: D
options.text: RNA ligase must first join each base

questions.why: Conventional target-specific PCR relies on primers that base-pair with sequences flanking the target. If both flanks are unknown, it is difficult to define the ends of the intended product.

notes.A: Adenine provides an ordinary template base and can be copied by complementary incorporation.
notes.B: Whether a sequence has been determined does not change the phosphate backbone of its DNA.
notes.C: Heat separates the template strands in conventional PCR, so bacterial helicase activity is not required.
notes.D: Polymerase extends a primer by adding nucleotides. RNA ligase is not needed to join individual bases.

questions.stem: Which product is directly amplified in standard reverse-transcription PCR?
questions.why: Reverse transcriptase first makes DNA complementary to the RNA template. The amplification step copies that cDNA, because conventional PCR uses DNA as its immediate template.

notes.A: RNA translation can produce proteins, but that is not the amplification step in reverse-transcription PCR.
notes.C: Antibodies are proteins and are not template molecules for DNA polymerase.
notes.D: Phospholipid synthesis is a metabolic process rather than a product of reverse transcription.
notes.E: Collagen fibrils are extracellular protein structures and cannot act as templates for PCR.

questions.stem: What primarily determines DNA-fragment migration through an agarose gel under an electric field?
questions.why: DNA's negative backbone charge drives it towards the positive electrode. For comparable linear DNA fragments, the agarose matrix impedes longer fragments more strongly, so shorter fragments generally travel farther.

notes.A: An open reading frame is a feature of sequence interpretation and does not determine size-based mobility.
notes.B: Fragment migration here concerns purified DNA, not the amino acid content of associated proteins.
notes.C: Cytosine methylation can affect some DNA properties, but size is the main determinant under standard conditions.
notes.E: RNA polymerase concentration is not needed to drive migration of DNA through an agarose gel.

questions.stem: Which technique identifies a specific DNA fragment after electrophoresis and probe hybridization?
questions.why: Southern blotting separates DNA fragments and transfers them to a membrane. A labelled complementary probe detects the fragment containing the sequence of interest.

notes.B: Northern blotting is the corresponding hybridisation method for detecting RNA rather than DNA.
notes.C: Western blotting uses antibodies to detect proteins separated by electrophoresis.
notes.D: ELISA measures antigen or antibody binding in a different assay format without identifying separated DNA fragments.
notes.E: Flow cytometry measures properties of individual particles or cells rather than identifying DNA fragments on a blot.

questions.stem: Which laboratory blotting technique is most appropriate for detecting a specific RNA transcript?
questions.why: Northern blotting separates RNA and transfers it to a membrane. A complementary probe identifies the desired transcript and can provide information about its size.

notes.A: Southern blotting uses a probe to detect DNA fragments, rather than an RNA transcript.
notes.B: Western blotting is an antibody-based method for detection of selected proteins.
notes.D: Immunofluorescence uses fluorescent antibody reagents and is not the standard blot for detecting a specified RNA transcript.
notes.E: A Coombs test detects red-cell-associated immunoglobulin or red-cell-reactive antibodies, not transcripts on a membrane.

questions.stem: What can a restriction fragment length polymorphism reveal in a genetic test?

options.label: A
options.text: A change only in antibody Fc sequence

options.label: B
options.text: A change in peptide charge without DNA

options.label: C
options.text: A change in serum albumin concentration

options.label: D
options.text: A change only in mitochondrial membrane

options.label: E
options.text: A change in DNA restriction-site pattern

questions.why: A DNA sequence change can create or remove a restriction site, changing the pattern of cut fragments. Some length variations between unchanged sites can also produce a restriction fragment length polymorphism.

notes.A: An antibody amino acid change is detected by this method only indirectly if an underlying DNA difference alters the fragment pattern.
notes.B: A change in protein charge is not itself measured by DNA restriction fragment analysis.
notes.C: Serum albumin concentration is a biochemical measurement and does not describe a DNA fragment polymorphism.
notes.D: Membrane structure is not the readout of a test that compares lengths of DNA fragments.

questions.stem: Which highly variable DNA markers are often compared for forensic profiling and paternity testing?
questions.why: Short tandem repeat loci vary in how many repeat units each allele carries. Comparing many such loci gives informative patterns for distinguishing individuals and evaluating relatedness.

notes.A: A uniform stop codon is less informative because it does not provide the repeat-length variation used for profiling.
notes.C: Highly conserved sequences tend to show less variation between individuals than selected STR loci.
notes.D: Identical promoters do not distinguish individuals, and mitochondrial markers do not directly track paternal inheritance.
notes.E: A single conserved housekeeping codon has far less discriminatory value than a panel of variable repeats.

questions.stem: How can DNA typing most decisively exclude a proposed biological father at an informative locus?

options.label: A
options.text: Child matches the putative father at several loci

options.label: B
options.text: Father and child share one STR allele

options.label: C
options.text: The mother carries both child alleles

options.label: D
options.text: A paternal allele is absent from the alleged father

options.label: E
options.text: The child carries one maternal allele

questions.why: At an informative locus, the child's allele that cannot be explained by the known mother is expected to come from the biological father. Its absence is exclusionary evidence that should be assessed with other loci and possible mutation or error.

notes.A: Multiple matching loci provide support for compatibility rather than directly excluding paternity.
notes.B: A shared allele is compatible with inheritance at that locus, although one match cannot establish paternity.
notes.C: A mother carrying both of the child's alleles may make it harder to identify the paternal allele unambiguously.
notes.E: One allele should normally come from the mother. This observation does not by itself implicate or exclude the alleged father.

questions.stem: Which application is a common use of gene-specific DNA probes in inherited disease testing?
questions.why: A probe can bind a complementary DNA sequence at a locus associated with inherited disease. If the assay distinguishes the relevant variant, the binding pattern can identify the pathogenic sequence.

notes.B: Plasma calcium is measured through chemical assays rather than by matching a DNA sequence.
notes.C: Platelet aggregation testing measures cellular clumping, not the presence of a known DNA variant.
notes.D: Hormone affinity concerns binding of a hormone to a receptor, a different measurement from sequence hybridisation.
notes.E: Serum thyroid hormone is commonly measured by biochemical immunoassays rather than a gene-specific DNA probe.

questions.stem: What distinguishes somatic gene therapy from germline genetic modification?

options.label: B
options.text: Germline changes affect only skin cells

options.label: C
options.text: Somatic changes are not intended to be inherited

options.label: D
options.text: Somatic modification cannot change protein expression

options.label: E
options.text: Somatic treatment does not involve DNA

questions.why: Somatic gene therapy aims to modify body cells to treat the recipient. Germline modification concerns reproductive cells or their precursors, so the change can be inherited by offspring.

notes.A: Reproductive cells are part of the germline. Somatic treatment targets other cells of the individual.
notes.B: Skin cells are somatic cells and do not define the germline.
notes.D: Altering expression or protein function can be a therapeutic aim of somatic modification.
notes.E: Somatic gene therapy can involve delivery or alteration of DNA. The decisive distinction is the intended cell lineage.

questions.stem: Which component of CRISPR-Cas gene editing most directly specifies the target sequence?
questions.why: A guide RNA contributes target specificity by pairing with a complementary DNA sequence. The associated Cas protein carries out the enzymatic action at a compatible target.

notes.A: Restriction fragment size can be measured after digestion but does not specify which target the Cas complex recognises.
notes.B: An Fc receptor binds an antibody constant region and is unrelated to recognition by an RNA guide.
notes.C: Exposed platelet phospholipids provide a coagulation surface rather than a signal for DNA targeting.
notes.D: Collagen glycine repeats determine a feature of protein structure and do not direct the Cas enzyme to a DNA sequence.

questions.stem: Which technique can rapidly produce many copies of one known DNA segment without cloning it in bacteria?
questions.why: Polymerase chain reaction repeatedly copies a defined DNA region outside living cells. Products can serve as templates in later cycles, so the amount rises rapidly without bacterial cloning.

notes.A: A Southern blot detects DNA fragments and does not multiply copies of the target sequence.
notes.C: Protein electrophoresis separates proteins rather than replicating a DNA segment.
notes.D: The direct Coombs test detects antibody or complement coating patient red cells.
notes.E: Plasmid selection distinguishes cells carrying a vector and does not directly perform cell-free amplification.

questions.stem: Why can a restriction site mutation be detected by comparing digested DNA fragment patterns?

options.label: A
options.text: Restriction enzymes read RNA codons only

options.label: B
options.text: Gel electrophoresis separates by antibody class

options.label: D
options.text: Different cut sites produce different lengths

options.label: E
options.text: DNA probes hybridize to similar fragments

questions.why: A DNA mutation can eliminate an existing restriction site or create a new one. Cutting at different positions changes the lengths of the resulting fragments, producing a different pattern.

notes.A: Restriction endonucleases recognise DNA motifs rather than reading codons in RNA.
notes.B: The electrophoretic comparison separates DNA fragments by their mobility, not by immunoglobulin class.
notes.C: Restriction enzymes cleave DNA and do not measure protein mass.
notes.E: A probe can identify a particular fragment, but the length change originates from altered restriction cleavage.
